item.title: Measuring the Influence of Modality-Specific Node Representations on Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.23863v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal attributed graphs combine graph structure with node text and image representations in recommendation and multimedia analysis. Graph predictors propagate these representations across connected nodes, so one input can change predictions at its own and nearby nodes. Measuring this distributed response reveals which modality-specific inputs a trained model relies on and how predictor design changes that reliance. We study influence measurement for modality-specific node representations. Given an encoded graph, a trained predictor, a training split, and fixed candidate representations, the task outputs one influence score per candidate and separate text and image rankings. We score a candidate by replacing it with its modality's training-node mean and comparing the original and changed predictions. Existing feature attribution and data valuation generally target one output, training examples, whole nodes, or graph elements rather than prediction changes across graph nodes. Our empirical study shows that nearby-node responses contain information missed by source-only scores and simple proxies, while response magnitude alone does not identify which class changes support the task. Guided by these observations, we propose MoGI (Modality-specific Graph Influence). It propagates training labels to define task direction, reads the same replacement response for the favored class and full class distribution, and averages the resulting ranks. MoGI requires no predictor retraining or learned scoring parameters. Under a shared five-dataset, eight-predictor benchmark, it achieves the largest aggregate held-out loss increase against all five external methods at every tested ranking cutoff.
item.dc:creator: Xu Wang, Xunkai Li, Yinlin Zhu, Rong-Hua Li

item.title: TeleTwin: A Calibrated Digital Twin of Telegram Crisis Discourse as a Ground-Truth Testbed for Detecting LLM-Powered Information Operations
item.description: arXiv:2610.23944v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models make it cheap to run influence operations whose messages never repeat, yet real platforms offer almost no ground truth for testing whether coordination detectors can find them. The problem is sharpest on Telegram, which moderates little and spreads content through broadcast channels and forwarding rather than a follow graph. We introduce TeleTwin, an LLM-powered digital twin of a Telegram crisis-discourse ecosystem in which channels are agents, each instantiated from the history of a real channel, calibrated on 1.07 million messages from 195 public channels on the Israel-Gaza and Iran-Israel conflict (March-August 2025). On a held-out period containing the June 2025 Iran-Israel war, the twin tracks daily dynamics better than statistical baselines (correlation 0.86 against 0.64) and reacts to the war unprompted, but it over-focuses on the conflict, over-amplifies forwarding cascades, underestimates the shock and writes recognisably LLM-like text. We then inject LLM-written campaigns with known membership into the real data and into the twin. In real data, identical-text, co-URL and synchrony detectors fail once a campaign rewords, staggers or drops links; multilingual semantic similarity recovers loud campaigns, including cross-lingual ones, but not quiet ones, and its false positives fall unevenly across political perspectives. Inside the twin all detectors fail, because the simulated background is about 40 times more semantically homogeneous than the real one. Digital twins can supply ground truth for campaigns, but not, without calibrating their diversity, a realistic background for evaluating semantic detectors.
item.dc:creator: Despoina Antonakaki, Sotiris Ioannidis

item.title: Duration-Aware Dissimilarity in Temporal Networks
item.description: arXiv:2610.23978v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Temporal-network comparison becomes substantially more challenging when interactions are associated with explicit traversal times, since both event timing and duration determine temporal reachability and journey performance. We introduce a duration-aware dissimilarity framework for temporal networks whose edges carry departure times and traversal durations. The proposed approach compares networks through source-specific temporal-distance profiles using the $1$-Wasserstein distance, thereby retaining both temporal information and source correspondence. We evaluate the framework on real public-transport timetable networks under controlled schedule delays, duration-aware randomized reference models, and naturally occurring temporal variations. We further benchmark the proposed measure against existing path-based temporal dissimilarity approaches under the same perturbation scenarios. The results show that the proposed representation responds consistently to both the extent and the magnitude of temporal disruption, while retaining distinctions that may be compressed by contact- or hop-based temporal summaries. Overall, the findings support duration-aware temporal distances as a useful basis for comparing temporal systems in which traversal and waiting times directly affect network performance.
item.dc:creator: Giuseppe F. Italiano, Anna Mpanti

item.title: Modeling Group Socialization in Online Communities
item.description: arXiv:2610.24140v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Newcomers to online communities must learn a group's norms to participate successfully. This process is known as socialization, and has been the subject of considerable study in the online communities literature. Foundational work on group socialization in social psychology, however, suggests that socialization is actually a bidirectional process: individuals and communities adapt to each other's needs. In this work we develop a formal quantitative model of socialization, and present the first large scale empirical validation of the bidirectional socialization hypothesis using Reddit data. More specifically, we focus on linguistic socialization, and model users' comments in online communities as a mixture of in-group language and language from ``background'' communities they previously participated in. On a dataset of 112 subreddits (7.8 million tokens) find that our bidirectional model makes predictions that better generalize across users and time than two unidirectional socialization models. Furthermore, we conduct a qualitative analysis in which we demonstrate that our model is able to extract interpretable socialization patterns from the data that align with the existing literature. Specifically our model is able to learn that users conform more to group norms in topically niche communities with stricter content moderation rules, and that long time users conform more than newcomers. We emphasize that the claims made in this paper are explicitly falsifiable -- we are staking out a clear claim about what the socialization process looks like, and encourage future work to challenge our model.
item.dc:creator: Vinay Koshy, Iris Zhong, Karrie Karahalios, Benjamin Mako Hill, Amy X. Zhang

item.title: Source Attribution and Audience Uptake in Digital Witnessing: Evidence from a Chinese Diaspora Account on X
item.description: arXiv:2610.24269v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital-witnessing research explains how citizen testimony becomes publicly visible. Less is known about audience uptake after publication and whether the attributed source corresponds to the form of response. This study analyzes 47,635 posts (April 2022 to May 2026) from Teacher Li Is Not Your Teacher, a diaspora-based account that curates and publishes reports and testimony from inside China for transnational audiences. Among 25,093 witness-relevant posts, 3,601 explicitly attribute their material to ordinary submitters. These posts receive more replies than other witness-relevant posts across adjusted analyses and show a more reply-oriented profile. The primary doubly robust retweet estimate is near zero. Among audited replies to November 2022 user-submitted posts, 91.4% substantively engage the focal material. The pattern is consistent with ordinary-person source attribution presenting testimony as situated and open to public response. The study extends digital witnessing beyond visibility by separating redistribution from the public response that gathers around testimony.
item.dc:creator: Huiqian Lai, Runze Ding

item.title: YouTube Clips and Broad but Shallow Attention to Candidates: Evidence from the 2024 Tokyo Gubernatorial Election
item.description: arXiv:2610.24387v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Video-sharing platforms and social media have gained influence in election campaigns, and third-party edited videos (called kirinuki in Japanese; hereafter, "clip videos") in particular have attracted attention. In Japan, Shinji Ishimaru, previously unknown nationally, finished second in the 2024 Tokyo gubernatorial election, a result widely attributed to his popularity on YouTube. Focusing on this case, we analyzed 44,331 YouTube videos relating to the nine leading candidates, posted between July 5, 2020, and July 7, 2024. Using cumulative views and engagement data as of June 25, 2025, we examined the relationship between clip videos and the attention candidates received. Regression analyses with standard errors clustered by channel showed that Ishimaru, the most watched candidate, did not draw the most active engagement. Videos mentioning Ishimaru received about 36% fewer likes and 41% fewer comments at the same number of views, whereas some candidates with fewer views recorded higher engagement rates. Clip videos were associated with this breadth of attention. They received about 1.8 times more views but 26% fewer comments at the same number of views, and mentions of Ishimaru were associated with about 2.6 times more views among non-clip videos. The interaction between the two, however, was not significant, and understanding the prominence of Ishimaru's cumulative views requires considering both the number of clip videos about him and the views per video. These results suggest that the spread of attention through clip videos may have functioned as a broad but shallow pathway, distinct from the formation of committed support.
item.dc:creator: Yoshito Miwa, Kazutoshi Sasahara

item.title: Scam Town: Can Scam Education Spread Like a Vaccine?
item.description: arXiv:2610.25040v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Most older adults who hear a warning about scams hear it from someone they know: a relative, a neighbour, or a friend who was targeted. Yet research on scam prevention almost always studies one person at a time. We ask whether scam awareness can spread through a community and protect it the way a vaccine does, since a warning protects whoever hears it and can be passed on. To find out, we built Scam Town, a simulated community in which a large language model plays each resident. Scam centres phone the residents, and after a call a resident can warn the people they know. Word of mouth helped, but it did not take off on its own: each warning led to fewer than one more, so a community cannot count on warnings "going viral". Across 80 simulated towns, everyday talk cut the number of people scammed by roughly a fifth. The largest gains came when an official warning, from a bank, a senior centre, or an agency, reached most of a town and residents then talked about it: in simulation (a combination we did not test live) the two together cut scams by about half. Protection was greatest when warnings reached the people scammers actually call, who here were older residents. Because our residents are language-model stand-ins rather than real people, we treat these findings as predictions to test with people, not as proof. They point to a simple recipe for scam education: give people a clear story they can retell, design campaigns to be passed along, and reach first those most likely to be called.
item.dc:creator: Simiao Ren, Tommy Duong, Xingyu Shen, Jiaqi Gan, Tsang Ng, Ankit Raj, Kidus Zewde, Huaiyu Guo, Siyu Zhang

item.title: A Theoretical Perspective on Link Prediction Heuristics
item.description: arXiv:2610.25686v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In network analysis, nodes with different degrees are usually weighted differently in tasks such as link prediction. For example, two individuals connected to the same high-degree node (e.g., a celebrity) are often considered less likely to know each other than if they share a low-degree connection. In this paper, we theoretically justify the reasoning behind this heuristic using a graph generation model. In this model, nodes are embedded in a latent metric space, and edges are more likely to form between nearby nodes. We analytically derive degree-based weighting schemes for commonly used link prediction and similarity measures. In particular, we identify the optimal weighting scheme for the Common Neighbors index and extend our analysis to other popular heuristics, including the graph distance. Our theoretical findings align with previous empirical observations, and we further validate them through experiments on both synthetic and real-world networks.
item.dc:creator: Jiajie Shi, David A. Meyer

item.title: Optimizing Marketing Budgets for Social Influence: A Generalized Fractional Incentives Framework
item.description: arXiv:2610.25823v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Marketing managers routinely allocate limited budgets across individuals in social networks whose responsiveness and influence vary substantially. We study the problem of Budgeted Generalized Fractional Influence Maximization (BGFIM), which captures the allocation of continuous levels of marketing spend across users in the presence of heterogeneous response and network spillovers. In this framework, adoption probabilities are governed by user-specific response functions that capture both baseline propensity and marginal responsiveness, while incentive costs vary across users. We propose a scalable solution approach based on a discrete greedy procedure with provable approximation guarantees, enabling tractable optimization under realistic budget constraints. Our formulation generalizes prior influence maximization models by allowing heterogeneous response and cost structures, providing a more flexible representation of targeted marketing interventions. Using experiments on multiple large-scale networks, we show that continuous allocation strategies can outperform standard heuristics and improve influence outcomes under heterogeneous conditions, and we illustrate how the framework can support profit-oriented decision making by identifying budget levels that balance marginal returns and costs. Overall, our results highlight the value of fine-grained budget allocation in networked marketing environments and offer a scalable approach for data-driven marketing resource allocation.
item.dc:creator: Abhishek K. Umrawal, Akhil Bhimaraju, Eliot W. Robson, Lav R. Varshney

item.title: Where Does Rhetorical Distortion Live? A Multi-Platform, Multi-Language Measurement of Influencer Content
item.description: arXiv:2610.26412v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Much of the manipulation in online influencer content is not false but disproportionate: an accurate fact is framed as historic, urgent, or catastrophic. Fact-checking and clickbait detection are not designed to capture such framing, and little is known about where it originates: with the creator, the topic, the platform, or the audience that replies. We operationalize rhetorical distortion through five literature-grounded dimensions (Significance Inflation, Anxiety Manufacturing, Novelty Claims, Loaded Language, and Temporal Distortion) and measure it with a three-tier pipeline in which bilingual lexical rules propose candidates, negative filters cancel known false-positive contexts, and an LLM verifies or relabels the candidates. Applying the pipeline to 13,060 posts from 330 accounts on six platforms (RSS/newsletters, YouTube, Bluesky, Reddit, Weibo, and X/Twitter), we find that platform is far more strongly associated with account-level distortion than content category (Kruskal-Wallis $\varepsilon^2=0.33$; two-way ANOVA $\eta_p^2=0.49$ for platform vs. $0.09$ for category). X/Twitter scores highest (DI 7.74 vs. 0.78 for RSS). Classifying tweets and their replies separately shows where this comes from: the reply layer readers see under a post (its top-5 replies) carries 3.5x the distortion of the tweet it answers (7.65 vs. 2.17, $p<10^{-6}$, 36 of 43 accounts), driven by Loaded Language. At equal text length the gap shrinks to 1.5x but remains significant, and creator tweets alone are statistically indistinguishable from YouTube and Bluesky. Two independent human annotators confirm the reply gap, and the platform ordering and the reply gap replicate with GPT-4o as a second classifier. On threaded platforms, measured distortion thus lives largely in the audience layer, which motivates measurement that separates creator and reply text.
item.dc:creator: Xucheng Yu, Jiangping Chen, Haohan Wang

item.title: What Remains Without Test Labels? Re-evaluating a Graph-Level Anomaly Detection Benchmark
item.description: arXiv:2610.24045v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Graph-level anomaly detectors are trained only on normal graphs, yet benchmarks may use test labels for model selection. We examine whether UB-GOLD results reused by later papers support label-free detection. We audit UB-GOLD and 14 GLAD code bases, re-run 21 detectors on UB-GOLD's folds under selection rules with and without test labels, and evaluate sensitivity to known structural changes. Test labels select checkpoints in UB-GOLD's shared training loop and checkpoints or hyperparameters in 8 of the 14 code bases. UB-GOLD also evaluates its kernel baselines against misaligned labels. Across nine datasets, selecting checkpoints by test AUROC adds an average of 5.12 AUROC points [3.97, 6.24] for the 12 UB-GOLD detectors relative to the final checkpoint and 4.13 [3.32, 4.79] relative to held-out normal graphs. In a post hoc permutation analysis with no truly better checkpoint, picking the best of noisy test evaluations still yields a gain more than half as large as the one observed against the final checkpoint. Configurations tuned on test labels score a further 1.53 points [0.64, 2.42] above repository defaults, a gap that mixes the value of test labels with that of tuning itself. With tuned hyperparameters and label-free checkpoint selection, the two strongest detectors retain their lead, while comparisons below them are less stable. Six of eight detectors evaluated out of sample miss size-preserving composition changes that graphlet counts detect. We recommend reporting results selected without test labels as the main comparisons and release per-run outputs that allow verification without retraining.
item.dc:creator: Yujie Lu, Da Yan

item.title: Location, Location, Generation: Where You Ask Matters for Generative Engine Optimization
item.description: arXiv:2610.24081v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative search engines answer local and commercial questions with a written answer and a few cited sources. A growing practice of generative engine optimization (GEO) monitors which sources and brands these answers show, typically from a single place. In this paper, we present a controlled audit of how the user's location changes the sources that generative engines cite. We ask 300 questions of ChatGPT with 19 declared locations, and of ChatGPT and Gemini from five network locations, each twice to measure run-to-run noise (31,200 answers). The engines take location from different channels. ChatGPT follows the location an application declares, down to the city: it writes the place into its own searches, and its search backend localizes results even when the queries name no place. It ignores the network. Gemini ignores the declared location and follows the country of the network, changing most of its sources even for questions that do not depend on place. The businesses the answers recommend change with the sources. Thus, visibility in generative search is specific to the user's location, and audits must control both channels.
item.dc:creator: Mahe Chen, Nick Koudas

item.title: The Kemeny-Braess Paradox in Random Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.24143v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In 2016, Kirkland and Zeng initiated the mathematical treatment of Braess paradox for random walks on graphs using Kemeny's constant as the measure of travel time. We study this phenomenon for the Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi random graph $G(n,p)$. An edge in a connected graph is called Kemeny-Braess if its deletion preserves connectedness and decreases Kemeny's constant, while a nonedge is Kemeny-Braess if its insertion increases Kemeny's constant. Let $\bar d=(n-1)p$ be the expected degree of $G\sim G(n,p)$, and assume that $\bar d-\log n\to\infty$, so that $G$ is connected with high probability. We determine the sharp asymptotic thresholds for the existence of both types of paradoxical behaviour. With $C^*=1/(1-\log 2)$, the threshold for Kemeny-Braess edges is $\bar d=C^*\log n$, whereas the threshold for Kemeny-Braess nonedges is $\bar d=2C^*\log n$. Hence, as the expected degree $\bar d$ increases, the connected regime exhibits three phases: first Kemeny-Braess paradox occurs for both edges and nonedges, then only for nonedges, and finally it disappears. In particular, in the dense regime, with high probability $G$ has no Kemeny-Braess edges or nonedges. This contrasts sharply with the spectral gap of the normalised Laplacian, for which Braess' paradox persists at constant edge density. Our proof combines a spectral-moment expansion of Kemeny's constant with uniform edge-perturbation estimates. Near the thresholds, the sign of the perturbation is governed by the endpoint degrees, and binomial large deviations yield the constant $C^*$ and the factor of two between the two thresholds.
item.dc:creator: Manuel Bodirsky, Lorenzo Ciardo, Mihyun Kang

item.title: Strategic Origins of Network Structure
item.description: arXiv:2610.24792v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The structure and dynamics of complex networks are intimately linked. Despite immense progress in statistically characterizing these systems, a generalized mechanistic framework explaining why specific mesoscale structures emerge remains elusive. Here we introduce the game-graph equilibrium, the stable rest point of a payoff-driven partner-choice dynamic, analogous to a Nash equilibrium. This reveals network structure as the fossilized record of strategic interaction. We prove analytically that two-type games have exactly four network topologies, which are their exhaustive thermodynamic phases: assortative, disassortative, and two core-peripheries. This result generalizes to $K^K$ topological classes for $K$-type interactions. Furthermore, four distinct Nash equilibria produce core-periphery topologies, yet their payoffs reveal whether the underlying dynamic is cooperative or exploitative. To recover the generating dynamics from observed networks, we develop mechanistic inference by constraining a block model to lie on a low-dimensional, game-theoretic manifold. Applied to real-world networks, the model yields interpretable quantities, distinguishes states that look identical to conventional methods, predicts network topologies it has never seen without retraining, and controls its own complexity without hand-tuned penalties. Networks such as international trade are well described by the model despite the hard constraint, suggesting that real-world systems are organized by payoff-driven partner choice. Our framework resolves a foundational ambiguity by offering a precise, mechanistic definition of communities: strategic equivalence.
item.dc:creator: Christoph Riedl, Rory Smead

item.title: A general mechanism for collective foraging: percolating recruitment cascades coupled to a maximum-entropy
item.description: arXiv:2610.24865v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Foraging recruitment is a contagion: an agent finding a resource triggers a linear-threshold cascade -- the model for rumour and adoption spread on social networks -- embedded in space. Because activation is degree-normalized, the same rule that spreads the cascade also stifles it as neighbourhoods crowd (density-dependent blocking), so the swarm aggregates on a resource, then releases to explore again. The cascade runs on the communication network, but acting on it moves agents in physical space, and that motion rewires the network: network and physical space are one coupled system, and this feedback -- not tuning -- makes the coordination self-limiting. Because recruitment chains along the graph rather than near neighbours alone, whether a discovery stays local or spans the swarm is a matter of percolation, and past a critical connectivity the swarm holds itself in a cascade window -- locally near-critical though globally subcritical, a self-organized, sandpile-like drive-avalanche cycle. Nothing is tuned, yet behaviours foraging biology documents separately emerge together -- recruitment, marginal-value patch-leaving, and Levy search with a switch to local exploitation. These are not coincidences but one least-committal principle: the resource field and the search both follow from maximum entropy -- Levy search matched to the field's sparsity, recruitment to its clustering, so active-matter order and optimal foraging are one system in two domains. The gains are real but conditional: up to 7.6x the harvest of solitary search when resources are sparse and clustered, shrinking to nothing when search is already easy. Percolating cascades yield a large return on minimal communication. And that sparse, clustered field is the generic one -- resources almost inevitably aggregate, and maximum entropy makes it the least-committal one once they do -- so one untuned rule should recur widely.
item.dc:creator: Galen J. Wilkerson

item.title: Self-organizing reinforcement learning: a swarm approaches the explore-exploit optimum
item.description: arXiv:2610.25113v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The explore/exploit trade-off is the core problem of reinforcement learning (RL). We show that a minimal foraging swarm approaches its optimum - the ideal-free / Nash allocation of a multi-agent resource-sharing game (an equilibrium, not a return maximum) - with no learner and no reward signal. Agents explore by heavy-tailed (Levy) flights, recruit neighbours to a discovery through a threshold cascade on their proximity network, and disperse as a patch crowds; this cascade cycle balances exploration and exploitation and drives foragers toward the ideal free distribution. The swarm attains the shape of this optimum (committed foragers track richness with slope 0.94) but not its exact equilibrium - it stays measurably exploitable - reaching it dynamically (~150 steps) through the coupling of recruitment to movement: remove the coupling and matching collapses (0.94 -> 0.08). The RL sits at the level of the problem and the allocation reached, not the micro-rule: no step evaluates payoff (reward-free by construction, though the crowd signal is informationally tied to payoff), and the swarm reaches the allocation without learning it (quality plateaus and re-settles after resources move, no cumulative gain). Against a trained baseline the comparison is two-sided: in an easier, disembodied game a learner is more precise, while in the same embodied environment the reward-free swarm reaches ~65% of a validated oracle ceiling at zero training and leads until trained PPO and centralised-critic (CTDE) learners overtake it (~74-75%, 16 seeds, all above the swarm mean) after ~4,000 of 15,000 training steps - its advantage is in budget, not asymptote. In this one setting we read it not as beating RL but as a strong zero-shot, reward-free operating point: a demonstration that the self-organizing physics of a minimal swarm can carry a collective close to the optimum RL seeks, with none of RL's machinery.
item.dc:creator: Galen J. Wilkerson

item.title: Monte Carlo Experiments of Network Effects in Randomized Controlled Trials
item.description: arXiv:2312.01607v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies Monte Carlo simulations of content production in Randomized Controlled Trials on social networks modeled as random Watts-Strogatz graphs. Because treatment nodes are surrounded by control nodes, they do not receive the network boost they would receive if the entire network were treated, and part of their boost leaks into control. As a result, the treatment versus control lift underestimates the effect of a full graph-wide rollout. Clustering the treatment group reduces this underestimate, while its size does not depend on the size of the treatment group. These mechanisms appear as seven effects, each captured by a metric: the network effect, spillover effect, experiment dampening effect, intrinsic dampening effect, clustering effect, degree distribution effect and the experiment size effect.
item.dc:creator: M\'arton Trencs\'eni

item.title: Accelerating Spanning-Centrality Approximation with Sampling-Aware Vectorized Random Walks
item.description: arXiv:2410.14056v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Spanning centrality quantifies an edge's importance through its share of a graph's spanning trees, and approximating it for all edges (AESC) requires processing large volumes of irregular random walks under a prescribed error bound. Its applications include phylogenetic analysis and network robustness assessment. We focus on this random-walk processing bottleneck and propose Sampling-Aware Bouquet Arrangement (SABA), a CPU sampling and scheduling scheme that orders walks initialized on a uniform grid so that adjacent walks execute together in SIMD-width groups, called bouquets. For fixed per-walk random inputs, the ordering preserves the multiset of sampled walks while improving locality during neighbor access. On synthetic benchmarks, SABA achieves geometric-mean speedups of 6.95x and 7.41x over traditional random-walk generation for 2,048 and 16,384 walks per vertex, respectively, and up to approximately 49x in the latter setting. Within AESC, the complete 16-thread SABA implementation is 58.23x faster than the original single-threaded TGT+ implementation on average.
item.dc:creator: G\"okhan G\"okt\"urk, Kamer Kaya

item.title: Limits of Predictability in Civil Litigation
item.description: arXiv:2605.06151v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Lawyers, insurers, and litigation funders forecast how civil lawsuits will end, and legal theory distinguishes easy cases, in which the law determines the result, from hard cases, in which it does not. Yet there is little evidence on how accurately the outcome of a lawsuit can be forecast from the court record while the case is pending. We provide such evidence at scale. Using 835,190 filings and orders from 102,721 federal and state civil cases in 12 U.S. states, we estimate at each filing the probability that a case ends in a plaintiff win, a plaintiff loss, or a settlement, using only the record available then. The forecasts draw on structured information extracted from each filing, on comparable earlier cases and how they were resolved, a comparison practitioners make from experience and language models now make systematic, and on case histories of judges and law firms. We measure how predictable a case is by how concentrated its forecast is on a single outcome. Predictability varies across disputes: tort cases are the most predictable, and state-court cases are more predictable than federal ones, whereas business and corporate, intellectual-property, and property disputes and cases involving corporate parties are the least. Overall, 61 percent of forecasts are correct, rising to 95-97 percent when a win or a loss is given more than 90 percent probability. Richer information on facts, judges, and counsel improves forecasts for predictable cases but adds little for unpredictable ones. Holding case length fixed, forecasts do not sharpen as the record grows, and longer cases are harder to predict from the outset. Settlement is most frequent at intermediate predictability. The results provide a benchmark for how predictable civil litigation is, lay the groundwork for an empirical approach to legal indeterminacy, and show where forecasts could narrow information gaps between litigants.
item.dc:creator: Sandro Claudio Lera, Shahrokh Firouzi, Jonathan Habshush, Robert Mahari

item.title: I CAN Debias: Uncovering and Enhancing Self-debiasing Mechanisms of Social Bias in LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2605.09647v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As LLMs rapidly advance and become increasingly agentic, mitigating social bias and ensuring fairness at scale have become critical challenges. Prior work has shown that LLMs exhibit an emergent self-debiasing capability-an intrinsic mechanism that enables them to avoid generating biased outputs-but this mechanism remains poorly understood, leaving existing bias-mitigation approaches heavily reliant on carefully curated prompts or inefficient training procedures that risk catastrophic forgetting. To address this gap, we propose I-CAN-Debias, a unified framework for uncovering and enhancing self-debiasing mechanisms in LLMs through behavior-grounded Consistency-contrast-Aware Neuron analysis, which defines self-debiasing neurons not by the magnitude of their responses to biased inputs but by activation patterns that distinguish successful debiasing from biased failures. Using I-CAN-Debias, we find that self-debiasing neurons account for less than 2% of model parameters yet are causally critical: deactivating them raises the biased-response rate above 95%. These neurons cluster in the query and value projections of later layers and exhibit highly asymmetric cross-category transferability. Furthermore, targeted fine-tuning of these neurons substantially improves fairness while preserving general capabilities. Importantly, models tuned with I-CAN-Debias generalize robustly across diverse evaluations beyond the training distribution, spanning open-ended fairness, jailbreak attacks, and implicit bias, without requiring test-time debiasing prompts. Together, these findings provide new mechanistic insights and a parameter-efficient approach toward developing fair and trustworthy AI systems.
item.dc:creator: Jingshen Zhang, Bo Wang, Yanlin Fu, Yuewen Dang, Dongming Zhao, Yuexian Hou, Zifei Yu

item.title: The Effect of Expertise Signaling when Sharing Medical Information in Opinion Dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2610.16623v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Social media heavily influences health decisions, yet few opinion dynamics models account for how information is delivered. This work investigates how signaling source expertise shapes trust and long-term opinion formation. Through an online experiment, we find that adding a professional title to the sender's display name significantly increases a post's perceived credibility. Incorporating these findings to create a data-driven opinion dynamics model, we prove that (1) connecting users through some paths to an expert guarantees consensus with experts' opinion, while (2) higher rates of expertise signaling accelerate reaching consensus. Simulations show that (3) convincing even 20% of users to signal their title reduces consensus time to nearly one-third in Erdos-Renyi networks and (4) higher title adoption brings average opinion much closer to that of experts in scale-free and real-world networks. Altogether, our work highlights expertise signaling as a viable intervention to promote validated medical information online.
item.dc:creator: Moyi Li, Chuqiao Yan, Jesus Jair Reyes Gutierrez, Aleksandra Urman, Stefania Ionescu

item.title: Quotient Geometry and Persistence-Stable Metrics for Swarm Configurations
item.description: arXiv:2603.18041v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Can temporal information recover geometry lost by a persistence diagram? For $n\ge3$ points on the unit sphere evolving under known homogeneous complete consensus, we prove generic local recovery modulo rotations and permutations from two ordinary zero-dimensional Vietoris--Rips persistence snapshots. The structural result applies to every labeled tree: its edge inner products and their first temporal derivatives have differential rank $2n-3$, exactly the dimension of the regular formation quotient. An explicit pole--equator witness proves this simultaneously for all tree types after taking a finite intersection of open dense sets. Although one snapshot has generic local fibers of dimension $n-2$, two sufficiently close snapshots are injective on a common neighborhood. The optimal inverse Lipschitz constant grows as $\Theta(1/|h|)$ when the sampling interval tends to zero. A verified left inverse, interval derivative bounds, and explicit persistence-matching margins certify neighborhoods and time intervals at rational reference formations. The results are local and model-specific; reflection ambiguity and centered rank obstructions remain.

item.title: Bonsai: A class of effective methods for independent sampling of graph partitions
item.description: arXiv:2603.18347v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We develop effective methods for constructing an ensemble of district plans via independent sampling from a reasonable probability distribution on the space of graph partitions. We compare the performance of our algorithms to that of standard Markov Chain based algorithms in the context of grid graphs and state congressional and legislative maps. For the case of perfect population balance between districts, we provide an explicit description of the distribution from which our method samples.
item.dc:creator: Jeanne Clelland, Kristopher Tapp

item.title: Estimating the Social Cost of Corporate Data Breaches
item.description: arXiv:2603.21270v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: While the size of a data breach is typically measured by the number of (consumer, customer, or user) records exposed or compromised, its economic impact is generally measured from the point of view of the corporation suffering the data breach: cost in crisis management, legal fees, drop in stock price, and so on. This study examines whether it is possible to estimate the true cost, or the social cost of a data breach, measured by the impact on its victims and their out of pocket costs. To accomplish this we establish: (1) the estimation of the average direct financial losses of an identity theft (IDT) victim, including the opportunity cost of lost time, and healthcare expenditures associated with distress associated with identity theft; and (2) the estimation of increases in incidents of IDT that can be attributed to a major breach event. Our findings show that the average social cost per victim has declined significantly since 2016. Furthermore, we find that there is indeed a statistically significant increase in the number of IDTs following a mega-breach event when accounting for a discovery lag of 1-2 months post-breach. Applying our model to real-world cases allows us to estimate an upper and lower bound social cost of specific mega-breach events. We find that for the 2009 Heartland and 2013 Target breaches, even the conservative lower bound social cost estimate exceeded settlements by factors of 5 and 16, respectively. In contrast, the 2017 Equifax breach resulted in a lower bound estimate of $263.8 million, falling well within its $700 million settlement cap. While the Equifax upper bound estimate of $1.72 billion in social cost more than doubles this settlement, the narrowing gap between institutional liability and an incident's social cost provides empirical evidence of a market saturation effect that reduces the marginal damage of individual compromised records over time.
item.dc:creator: Lina Alkarmi, Armin Sarabi, Mingyan Liu

item.title: Belief Coevolution in a Social Network of Generalist and Specialist Large Language Models: A Controlled Study
item.description: arXiv:2607.27512v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in multi-agent environments. However, the processes by which beliefs form and propagate among interacting LLMs remain poorly understood. We introduce CoevolveSim, a framework for studying belief diffusion within networked LLM populations. CoevolveSim allows us to isolate and study three factors: domain specialization, social-role assignment, and social network structure. Within this framework, generalist and specialist LLM agents exchange and revise beliefs. In each round, an LLM agent observes a summary of its neighbors' beliefs before updating its own. We find that persona-style role assignment reshapes individual belief revision but has little effect on population-level consensus. In contrast, introducing finetuned specialist LLMs produces a large change in consensus and is accompanied by persistent asymmetries in outgoing influence. We further show that an opinion-dynamics surrogate combining individual persistence with population-level belief composition reproduces consensus with high fidelity in every scenario, whereas predicting individual final-round beliefs in heterogeneous LLM populations additionally benefits from agent identity.
